title: The Coffee Can

beats.text: One forgotten stock beat your whole managed portfolio.
Nineteen fifties. You manage a wealthy woman's money.
For about ten years, you buy, sell, trim, rebalance.
Then her husband dies, and his stocks land on your desk.
He'd been copying you. Half of you.
Whenever you said buy, he put in about five thousand dollars,
dropped the certificate in a safe deposit box, and forgot it.
So how did your lazy copycat do?
Some shrank below two thousand dollars. Several grew past a hundred thousand.
You see, it's the Old West coffee can under the mattress.
A dud can only lose what's inside. A winner has no ceiling.
One small bet in a company called Haloid grew past eight hundred thousand dollars.
Haloid became Xerox. That one stock outgrew his wife's whole portfolio. Yours.

facts.claim: Story told by money manager Robert G. Kirby in 'The Coffee Can Portfolio', Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 1984
It happened in the 1950s at an investment counsel firm; Kirby managed a woman client's money
Kirby had worked with her for about ten years when her husband suddenly died
The husband had followed Kirby's buy recommendations, putting about $5,000 into each
He put each certificate in his safe-deposit box and forgot it
He paid no attention to the sale recommendations
Some holdings were worth less than $2,000; several were worth more than $100,000
One jumbo holding worth over $800,000 came from a small commitment in Haloid, which became Xerox, and exceeded the total value of the wife's portfolio
The name alludes to the Old West, when people kept valuables in a coffee can under the mattress

caption:
1950s: a money manager's client lost her husband, and he found the man had been quietly copying his buy advice: about $5,000 a stock, certificate in the safe-deposit box, every sell ignored.
One small Haloid stake, later Xerox, was worth over $800,000, more than her whole managed portfolio. Robert Kirby called it the Coffee Can Portfolio (1984).
